reason: The wording is real and the verifier's date is defensible, but the verifier did not find the thing that matters about this maxim, and the citation as written will read as an error to anyone who checks it. WHAT I DID. I read PG 3351 (Letters to His Son, 1746-47) and confirmed the sentence under the heading BATH, October 9, O. S. 1746: In truth, whatever is worth doing at all, is worth doing well; and nothing can be done well without attention: I therefore carry the necessity of attention down to the lowest things, even to dancing and dress. Character for character as proposed. I then checked the reference tradition, and it disagrees: Wikiquote and Bartlett's both date this maxim to 10 March 1746. So I went to the 1774 first edition itself (archive.org bim_eighteenth-century_letters-written-by-the-l_chesterfield-philip-dor_1774_1_4) and searched the whole volume. THE MAXIM IS IN CHESTERFIELD TWICE, IN TWO DIFFERENT LETTERS. (a) LETTER LXXXVII, Dublin Castle, March the 10th, 1746: There is no surer sign in the world of a little, weak mind, than inattention. Whatever is worth doing at all, is worth doing well; and nothing call [can] be done well without attention. It is the sure answer of a fool ... This is the letter the reference works cite, and it has NO In truth and a FULL STOP after attention. (b) LETTER LXXXI, Bath, October 9th, O. S. 1746, running head 190 LORD CHESTERFIELD's LETTERS: ... requisite to make you agreeable and pleasing in society: In truth, whatever is worth doing at all, is worth doing well; and nothing can be done well without attention: I therefore carry the necessity of attention down to the lowest things ... This is the proposed wording, and its date is the one the verifier gives. WHAT THAT MEANS. The verifier is RIGHT and Bartlett's is wrong FOR THIS WORDING, which is a good outcome; but the citation says nothing about it, so the first editor or reader who looks the line up will find 10 March 1746 everywhere and think the card is misdated. A citation that is right and looks wrong is a liability on a track whose whole standard is verifiability, and the note is empty. WHY IT IS REFUTED, two grounds. (1) The line must carry the letter number, because the date alone does not distinguish two letters that both contain the maxim; Letter LXXXI is stable across the 1774 printings in a way a page number is not (in the scan I read it is vol. I, p. 190, but the 1774 edition exists in two-volume and four-volume settings). (2) The full stop after attention is a CUT: the October letter prints a colon and runs on into I therefore carry the necessity of attention down to the lowest things. The month's own practice notes such cuts (03-poet-01 on Folger printing no stop after nature, and 05-fict-02 in this same batch), and the note here is blank. Rule it CORRECTED with a note saying both things plainly: the original has a colon, not a full stop; and the maxim recurs without the In truth opening in the letter of 10 March 1746 from Dublin Castle, which is the date the reference works give. EVERYTHING ELSE HOLDS. Attribution is Chesterfield in his own voice, no character and no reporter. First published 1774 by Eugenia Stanhope, so pre-1999; it is a canonical eighteenth-century literary work, not modern self-help, and the volume's own index of subjects lists Whatever is worth doing at all, is worth doing well, which is the reference fame signal. shipped.js: not shipped, nothing near, Chesterfield 0 of 3, not banned.
